findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation
findings.body: The timeout context is derived from the incoming request context, so it is canceled as soon as the API request completes; the 10-second timeout does not detach it from that cancellation. Since these legacy writes run after the unified write returns, a client disconnect or normal request completion can cancel them before they finish. The same pattern is used for update, delete, and delete-collection, so successful unified writes can routinely fail to reach legacy storage.

findings.title: Legacy update recomputes the update against a different stored object
findings.body: Passing the original UpdatedObjectInfo to the legacy store causes it to compute the update again using the legacy object as its base, rather than writing the object produced by the successful unified update. The stores can have different state or resource versions, so an update can fail in legacy or produce a different result there. This loses the prior behavior of forwarding the unified result and undermines the dual write's purpose of keeping the stores aligned.

findings.title: Concurrent writes to one resource can reach legacy out of order
findings.body: Each mutation launches an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or serialization. If a create, update, and delete for the same object are handled in quick succession, the legacy calls can execute in a different order; for example, a delayed create can run after a delete and leave a deleted object in legacy storage. This can make legacy reads disagree with unified storage even when every individual legacy call succeeds.

findings.title: Delete metrics use object names as the kind label
findings.body: This call passes `name` where the other storage-duration calls pass the resource kind. If this argument supplies the metric's kind label, each deleted object creates a distinct label value, causing unbounded Prometheus time-series cardinality and making the delete metrics inconsistent with other operations.

findings.title: Legacy delete-collection results are recorded as storage metrics
findings.body: This asynchronous call records the legacy operation with `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy delete-collection latency and failures are attributed to unified storage. The same instrumentation mix-up occurs when storage create or update fails, where `recordLegacyDuration` is called instead. Monitoring will therefore misreport which backend is slow or failing.
